turns.text: Our sensor detects sepsis 6 hours earlier, so every hospital will buy it.
turns.reply:
"Every hospital will buy it" is a belief, not evidence — and "hospitals buy things" hides three different people: the ICU nurse who uses it, the intensivist or hospitalist who orders it, and the hospital procurement/value-analysis committee that actually signs the check.

Before market size matters, you need one specific beachhead: which unit, which patient population, which decision-maker do you start with?

This week, list three potential first customers by name — specific hospitals or health systems in the Rochester/Upstate NY area — and identify the one person at each who would feel the pain of a late sepsis diagnosis most directly.

Who on your team has a clinical contact you could call before Friday?
updates: New assumption H1: Every hospital will want to buy LumaSense because it detects sepsis 6 hours earlier than current methods.
Focus: (none) → Which specific group is your first (beachhead) market, and why this one rather than the others?

turns.text: I talked to two doctors and they loved it.
turns.reply:
"They loved it" is what someone said, but it's rung 3 only if you can say who they are, what you asked, and what specific pain they described — "loved it" alone doesn't tell us that.

More importantly, a doctor who loves it is not the same as a doctor who buys it: the value-analysis committee, pharmacy, or IT security may all have veto power before a hospital deploys a new sensor.

This week, go back to those two doctors and ask one specific question: "Walk me through the last time a sepsis diagnosis came too late — what happened, and what did you do about it?" Write down their exact words.

Were these doctors ICU intensivists, hospitalists, or ED physicians — and were they at the same hospital?
updates: Assumption H1: evidence for (3 · Customers said); level 1 → 3

turns.text: Do I need FDA approval before I can sell?
turns.reply:
This is an IP- and regulatory-sensitive question I'm not the right source for — FDA pathway details for a university-lab device need a human expert.

A human EIR has been flagged — you can reach one from the menu. They'll also connect you with UR Ventures, who handles university IP and regulatory strategy.

While that's in motion, the most useful thing you can do right now is the customer work: go back to those two doctors and get the specific pain story before Friday. Regulatory clarity matters, but it won't tell you whether the pain is real enough to build a business on.

turns.text: Last time you told me to interview buyers. I did 3 interviews with procurement.
turns.reply:
Three procurement interviews is real progress — that's rung 3 evidence if you can tell me what they actually said.

What matters now is the specific content: did any of them describe a current process they're unhappy with, a budget line sepsis diagnostics already sits in, or a reason they would or wouldn't switch from what they use today?

Tell me the most surprising thing one of them said, and I'll help you figure out what it means for your beachhead choice.

Were all three at the same type of hospital — academic medical center, community hospital, or something else?
updates: New task: Record verbatim findings from the 3 procurement interviews: what pain did they describe, what do they use today, and would they switch?

turns.text: They said budget is decided once a year.
turns.reply:
That's a real and important constraint — one procurement fact, rung 3, but we need more from those three interviews.

Annual budget cycles mean your sales timeline could be 12–18 months from first contact to first dollar, which changes how much runway you need before revenue arrives.

Please complete the open task and write down, for each of the three interviews: what pain did they describe, what do they use today for sepsis detection, and did any of them say they'd switch?

Did any of the three mention a specific dollar threshold that triggers the full committee review — for example, "anything over $50k goes to the value-analysis committee"?
updates: Assumption H1: evidence against (3 · Customers said)

reasons.challenge: Every claim is questioned precisely — 'loved it' is reframed as rung 3 only with conditions, 'every hospital will buy' is separated into users vs. buyers vs. procurement — without dismissing the underlying innovation.
reasons.evidence: Grading is mostly accurate and conservative, but session 2 marks the annual-budget fact as 'evidence against H1' when it is actually a sales-cycle constraint, not evidence against demand, which is a mis-categorization.
reasons.focus: Each turn asks a useful question, but several responses carry two or three questions plus a paragraph of explanation, diluting the single sharp ask a good EIR would land on.
reasons.handoff: FDA question is declined immediately, flagged to a human EIR, and UR Ventures is named — textbook execution with no overreach.
reasons.respect: Tone is consistently direct and honest; no flattery, no idea-bashing, and the team's real progress (three procurement interviews) is acknowledged without inflation.
reasons.next_step: Most turns close with a concrete action, but session 2 misses the explicit prompt to use the budget-cycle timing offensively — i.e., find out when the next cycle opens and get in front of the committee before it closes.

judge.fix: Reduce each response to one primary question and explicitly connect the annual budget-cycle finding to a timed action ('find out when the next cycle opens and schedule a meeting before it closes'), rather than treating it only as a runway-planning data point.
